title: Examining Student Interactions with a Pedagogical AI-Assistant for Essay Writing and their Impact on Students’ Writing Quality
venue: International Conference on Learning Analytics and Knowledge (LAK26)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how higher education students interact with a pedagogically designed generative AI essay-writing assistant and how those interaction patterns relate to writing quality. The authors argue that although prior research has examined general-purpose GenAI tools such as ChatGPT for writing support, less is known about how students use pedagogically grounded AI systems across the planning, drafting, and reviewing phases of writing, especially in undergraduate contexts. The study addresses two questions: whether distinct interaction patterns are associated with differences in essay quality, and how high- and low-performing students differ qualitatively in their AI-supported writing behaviors.

The intervention studied is an Essay Writing Assistant (EWA), a web-based GenAI tool built with pedagogical prompting informed by the INSPIRE model and effective tutoring principles. EWA was designed to support essay topic selection, outlining, drafting, and review without generating full essays for students. It incorporated contextual materials such as core readings and the scoring rubric, and used GPT-4.1-mini as the backend model. The researchers analyzed 1,282 coded interaction log instances using Sequential Pattern Mining and K-means clustering, then compared clusters on rubric-based essay scores with Mann-Whitney U tests. They also conducted qualitative analysis of interaction sequences in higher- and lower-writing-quality groups.

The study involved 32 undergraduate students from various majors enrolled in a university summer school. Students completed a 500-1000 word argumentative essay during a two-hour writing session on the topic of human-AI teaming in education. The task was part of course assessment, and students could use EWA, assigned readings, and X5Learn, but not other AI tools or peer communication. Essays were scored with a rubric covering content, analysis, organization and structure, quality of writing, and word limit; inter-rater agreement was high.

The main findings were that two broad interaction clusters emerged: one focused more on planning and essay structure, while the other focused more on content-related questioning. After multiple-comparison correction, no statistically significant score differences remained across clusters, but the planning/structure-oriented cluster showed a moderate effect size advantage in essay organization. Qualitative results suggested that students with higher writing quality used EWA more actively and iteratively: they asked questions, then submitted draft sections for feedback and revision. Lower-performing students tended to interact more passively by repeatedly asking for content or planning help without following up by writing. The authors conclude that pedagogically designed GenAI can support writing processes, but students benefit most when they actively use the system to refine their own drafts rather than only seeking answers.

identified_tools.name: Essay Writing Assistant (EWA)
identified_tools.description: A pedagogically prompted GenAI essay-writing assistant prototype designed to support argumentative writing through planning, drafting, and review without generating full drafts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by 32 undergraduate students during a two-hour argumentative essay-writing session; the study analyzed 1,282 interaction logs to examine how interaction patterns with EWA related to essay quality.

findings.finding_summary: Among 32 undergraduates using EWA in a two-hour writing session, K-means clustering of 1,282 coded interaction logs identified two behavior patterns: Cluster 1 emphasized outline planning and essay structure, while Cluster 2 emphasized content development. Mann-Whitney U tests with Holm correction found no statistically significant differences across essay dimensions after correction, but the Organization dimension showed a moderate effect size favoring Cluster 1 (M=3.42, Md=4, N=19) over Cluster 2 (M=2.77, Md=3, N=13), with U=74.5, Z=-2.03, p=0.04, adjusted p=0.16, r=0.36.
findings.measure: Argumentative essay rubric scores: content, analysis, organization, quality of writing

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative and sequential pattern analyses showed that students in the higher writing-quality cluster (n=21) more often displayed an active 'writing' pattern, submitting essay sections to EWA for feedback, whereas the lower writing-quality cluster (n=11) more often showed repeated question-asking patterns such as (hec,hec,hec) and (hep,hec) without follow-up writing. At 65% minsup, 'w' was a unique frequent pattern in the higher-quality group (support=14) and absent in the lower-quality group.
findings.measure: Clustered essay quality and sequential interaction patterns with EWA

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study with clustering, sequential pattern mining, qualitative analysis, and nonparametric comparisons, but it is not an RCT or strong quasi-experiment. The small sample (n=32) and observational design limit causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a moderate effect size in essay organization (r=0.36) associated with one EWA interaction pattern, although this did not remain statistically significant after Holm correction. Other effects were unclear or null, so overall impact is modest.
